Before you start

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Keep it light for ten seconds, then go straight to the next slide.

Slide 2 · Notes

If you ride, tell the story. Ask a few students for their version: a run, a swim against the current, walking home in a storm. Land on: we feel the headwind every second, and barely notice the tailwind.

Slide 3 · Notes

Keep it light. Ask: whose team got the hardest schedule this year? Everyone’s did. Seeing your tailwinds takes practice, and that’s the whole skill today.

Slide 4 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 5 · Notes

Three minutes, private. Then: “Hands up if you made at least one mark.” Most hands go up. “Everyone has some tailwinds. Most people have some headwinds too. Both are true at once.” Go first, with one of your own tailwinds.

Slide 6 · Notes

Click the picture; the clip plays four stretches of the film back to back, full screen. Press Esc to come back. Before: “Watch where the riders sit, and who’s working hardest.” L39ION is a pro team started by brothers Justin and Cory Williams, who grew up on 39th Street in South Los Angeles; the team mentors young riders.

Slide 7 · Notes

Ask for guesses first. Deep in a big pack, studies found riders need a small fraction of the effort of the leader.

Slide 8 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 9 · Notes

Say it calmly and plainly. Resumes with white-sounding names got about 50 percent more callbacks in one well-known study (Bertrand & Mullainathan, 2004). “Many white people never notice, because nobody notices a wind they don’t feel.” A white student’s real hardships are real too: race and money are different winds. Never ask a student of color to describe their headwinds.

Slide 10 · Notes

Two minutes. Keep it to everyday moments, not politics. Nobody shares their own headwinds.

Slide 11 · Notes

Take a few. If a student says “but I had it hard too,” agree: their headwinds are real, and both can be true.

Slide 12 · Notes

Say “not your fault” more than once. “You didn’t make the wind. You aren’t to blame for where you started. What you do with your tailwind is up to you.”

Slide 13 · Notes

Good riders take turns breaking the wind for the people behind them. Students write one way they could this week and keep the card. Share the take-home link.

Slide 14 · Notes

Watch for students carrying a lot. If this brought up something hard, a counselor is a good person to talk to.

Slide 15 · Notes

Share the take-home link.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why advantages are harder to notice than obstacles, name a few tailwinds of their own privately, describe race as one of the winds in American life, and choose one way to use a tailwind well. The lesson separates blame from responsibility on purpose: nobody is asked to feel guilty, and nobody is asked to share their own headwinds.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • Index cards, one per student
  • Speakers for a 4-minute clip (the Watch slide). Test it before class: it plays from YouTube, so YouTube can’t be blocked on your network.
  • The take-home link to share afterward

Flow

  1. 2 minRiding into the wind
  2. 2 minThe schedule guess: why we notice headwinds more
  3. 2 minEveryday tailwinds (private tally)
  4. 5 minWatch: L39ION racing in the pack
  5. 3 minDrafting, and race as one of the winds
  6. 3 minTurn and talk, share out
  7. 3 minBlame and responsibility, take a turn at the front, close

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

Riding into the wind, drafting in the pack, and take a turn at the front. Skip the clip, or send it to students afterward.

Before you teach
Go first, with one of your own tailwinds.

Something real and low-stakes: a parent who could help with homework, a car at sixteen, never being asked where you're really from. When the adult names a tailwind calmly, students learn it's something you can say out loud without falling apart.

Students of color are not the lesson.

Never ask a student to describe their headwinds or speak for a group, and don't let the room turn toward them. Tallies stay private. No privilege walk or any activity that lines students up by advantage: it ranks kids in front of each other.

Say "not your fault" more than once.

Separate blame from responsibility out loud, early and again at the end. Defensiveness drops when students hear they aren't being accused.

Expect "but I had it hard too."

Research finds that when white people hear about privilege, many respond by listing their hardships. Treat it as normal, not as an argument to win: "Your headwinds are real. You can have headwinds and tailwinds at the same time."

Race and money are different winds.

One study found that teaching about white privilege on its own made some people less sympathetic toward poor white people. Say clearly that a white student whose family is struggling has real headwinds, and that race and money are separate winds that can blow in different directions.

Keep it to everyday moments, not politics.

If a student says this is political, try: "Today we're looking at everyday moments, like who gets followed in a store. You can disagree with me. I'm asking you to notice." Don't debate policies or parties.

Watch for students carrying a lot.

A student who seems hurt, angry or shut down, or who describes being targeted for who they are, is worth a quiet check-in after advisory and a same-day note to a counselor.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Students of color.

Some will feel relief that this is named, some will feel tired of hearing it again, and some won't want attention on it at all. All three are fair. Give them the same choice to stay quiet that everyone else has.

White students with real headwinds.

Poverty, a disability, a family crisis, being LGBTQ+, a parent who's sick. The lesson only works if these are taken seriously alongside race.

Who counts as white is complicated.

Many Jewish, Middle Eastern and North African, Latino and multiracial students have a complicated relationship with the word white, and it can change depending on where they are. Let students name themselves, and don't sort anyone.

International and immigrant students.

Race works differently in other countries. A student may be in the majority at home and a minority here, or the other way around. That's a useful thing to notice, not a correction to make.

Families disagree about this.

Students come from homes with different politics and faiths. The lesson asks them to notice everyday moments, not to adopt a view. Respect disagreement, and keep dignity for everyone in the room.

Other tailwinds.

Money, citizenship, English at home, ability, gender, being straight or cisgender, parents who went to college. Name several so the idea is clear, then name race directly so it doesn't get lost.

Show who rides at the front.

If you use the L39ION clip, let it stand as a team at the top of its sport, not as a lesson about hardship. Justin Williams built it to widen who gets to see themselves in cycling.

What the research says

Across seven studies, people saw the obstacles they faced much more readily than the advantages that helped them, and this was explained by obstacles being easier to bring to mind.

Davidai & Gilovich, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2016

In wind tunnel and computer simulations of a 121-rider peloton, riders in the middle and back faced as little as 5 to 10 percent of the air resistance of a rider alone. Earlier research on small groups found drag reductions of roughly 30 to 50 percent.

Blocken et al., Journal of Wind Engineering and Industrial Aerodynamics, 2018

Fictional resumes with names common among white Americans received about 50 percent more callbacks than the same resumes with names common among Black Americans.

Bertrand & Mullainathan, American Economic Review, 2004

White participants shown evidence of racial privilege claimed more personal hardships; a short values affirmation reversed this, and affirmed participants acknowledged more personal privilege.

Phillips & Lowery, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 2015

White participants saw inequality as more threatening when it was framed as white advantage than as Black disadvantage; self-affirmation increased their acknowledgment of privilege.

Lowery, Knowles & Unzueta, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 2007

Among social liberals, reading about white privilege reduced sympathy for a poor white person and increased blame toward him, compared with a poor Black person.

Cooley et al., Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2019
